Fig. S3 Capacitance retentions of the positive and negative electrodes in SCs with 
varying m+/m- ratios: (a) 1; (b) 1.25; (c) 1.5; (d) 2
As shown in Fig. S3, capacitance retention of both electrodes decreases with 
increasing current density across all m+/m- ratios. The negative electrode exhibits 
superior capacitance retention relative to the positive electrode, attributable to its 
more ideal capacitive behavior within the operational potential window (Fig. 4). The 
capacitance retention differential (defined as R, i.e., capacitance retention of the 
negative electrode minus that of the positive electrode) progressively diminishes with 
increasing m+/m-. When the current density increases from 0.5 A·g⁻¹ to 20 A·g⁻¹, R 
decreases from 6.7% (m+/m- = 1) to 3.2% (m+/m- = 2). This convergence occurs 
because elevated m+/m- ratios optimize the positive electrode's operational potential 
range, enhancing its double-layer capacitive characteristics (Fig. 4). Critically, R 
remains below 7% across all tested configurations, confirming that all positive and 
negative electrodes in SCs exhibit similar rate capabilities. This effectively prevents 
the mass balance strategy from failing during the practical operation of SCs.
